That was the peace dividend: the money you get from buying 1% fewer explosions. Now here's the health dividend: what happens when you spend it on medicine.

Your species has a word for "health dividend," which implies that health is a bonus. On Wishonia, health is the default and disease is the bug report. On Earth, disease is the default and health is the dividend.

## The Queue

{{< var diseases_without_effective_treatment >}} have zero approved treatments. Not "in development." Not "awaiting funding." Zero. If you are diagnosed with one of them today, your treatment has not been invented. Nobody is working on it.

Your FDA approves roughly {{< var current_drug_approvals_per_year_nounit >}} new treatments per year. At that rate, the queue clears in approximately {{< var status_quo_queue_clearance_years >}}. For context, {{< var status_quo_queue_clearance_years >}} ago, your species had not yet invented writing. You were painting buffalo on cave walls and dying of tooth infections.

## What It Costs to Fix

![It'll cost 40 million to run this per year. Maybe 27 million, maybe 56 million. Either way, less than one fighter jet.](/assets/images/health-dividend/health-dividend-section-the-framework-cost-breakdown-bw-academic.jpg)

Your decentralized FDA will cost {{< var dfda_annual_opex >}} per year to operate. Servers, engineers, compliance, global integration. This is roughly what your species spends annually on Halloween costumes for dogs.

A system that could test cures for {{< var rare_diseases_count_global_nounit >}} diseases costs less to run than the outfits you put on animals that don't want to wear them. Less than one fighter jet. Less than what FIFA spends on "hospitality" (your word for bribing officials in a building with chandeliers).

## Why Your Trials Cost a Tesla Per Person

Traditional Phase III trials cost **{{< var traditional_phase3_cost_per_patient >}}** per patient. A Tesla. Per person. To find out if a pill works. The pill costs 37 cents to make. The paperwork weighs more than the patient.

Then the Oxford RECOVERY trial proved you can do the same thing for **{{< var recovery_trial_cost_per_patient >}}**. During a pandemic. While panicking. They tested COVID treatments on 40,000+ patients by:

Using existing hospital staff (doctors who were already treating patients and could presumably continue doing so while also writing things down), collecting data electronically (instead of sacrificing forests to the paperwork gods), and asking "does the patient live or die?" instead of "did they complete form 27-B in triplicate?" 

Scale that globally: up to **{{< var dfda_trial_cost_reduction_factor >}} cost reduction**. Same data quality. Your governments spend **{{< var global_government_clinical_trials_spending_annual >}} per year** on clinical trials [@global-government-clinical-trial-spending-estimate]. Industry adds another {{< var global_industry_clinical_trials_spending_annual >}}, mostly on drugs that are already profitable. Scale RECOVERY-style pragmatic trials across the full {{< var global_clinical_trials_spending_annual >}} market and you save up to **{{< var dfda_benefit_rd_only_annual >}} annually**. That's before counting the lives. I'm saving those for dramatic effect.

## What Changes for the Human Who Gets Sick

![With 58.6 billion, you could run 10,000 trials and address 7,000 rare diseases. Currently you're spending that much to run far fewer trials for common diseases. Priorities.](/assets/images/health-dividend/health-dividend-section-what-var-dfda-benefit-rd-only-annual-buys-you-bw-academic.jpg)

Right now, if you are diagnosed with one of those {{< var rare_diseases_count_global_nounit >}} untreated diseases, you enter a waiting room with no exit date. People die there. Not because a cure is impossible, but because nobody funded the trial. Your species spent the trial money on a submarine that hides underwater, which is useful if your enemy is a fish.

Each new drug approval is worth $1.62 billion [@arxiv-2212-07384] in market value. Your FDA approves roughly {{< var current_drug_approvals_per_year >}}. That is the speed at which a species with nuclear weapons and artificial intelligence has chosen to cure itself.

With {{< var dfda_trial_capacity_multiplier >}} more trial capacity, you could fund 10,000 new pragmatic clinical trials per year at $5M each (still luxurious by RECOVERY standards), test treatments for {{< var rare_diseases_count_global_nounit >}} rare diseases currently ignored because orphan diseases aren't profitable enough for your orphan-making economic system, cut development time from 17 years to 3-5 years (most terminal patients don't have 17 years; this has not occurred to anyone in charge), and make medicines affordable by eliminating {{< var pharma_drug_development_cost_current >}} development costs. Seventeen years. That's how long it currently takes to get a drug from "this probably works" to "you can have it." Your species figured out how to split atoms in 6 years during a war, but letting a cancer patient take a pill that passed safety testing requires the gestation period of three consecutive elephants.

## The Cost of Taking Your Time

Disease costs humanity **{{< var global_disease_economic_burden_annual >}} annually** in welfare losses ({{< var global_annual_daly_burden >}} avoidable DALYs at {{< var standard_economic_qaly_value_usd >}}/QALY [@ihme-gbd-2021]). The number is larger than global GDP ({{< var global_gdp_2025 >}}) because GDP measures market transactions, not the value of being alive and not in pain. The {{< var standard_economic_qaly_value_usd >}}/QALY figure is the standard rate governments already use when deciding whether to approve drugs, build highways, or regulate pollution.

Every day without this system costs **{{< var dfda_rd_savings_daily >}}** in wasted trial spending alone. Delayed treatments cost {{< var dfda_efficacy_lag_elimination_dalys >}} healthy life-years over the full lag period (cumulative across all deaths and disability during the delay, not a single year's burden). The regulatory lag is not a safety feature. It is a waiting room where people die. You just gave it a nicer name.

See [Daily Opportunity Cost of Inaction](https://dfda-impact.warondisease.org#daily-opportunity-cost-of-inaction) for calculations.

## The Return

![Conservative return on investment versus total return including not letting people die. One number is big, the other is astronomically big. Both beat war.](/assets/images/health-dividend/health-dividend-section-roi-scenarios-bw-academic.jpg)

Your decentralized FDA costs {{< var dfda_annual_opex >}}/year. It saves {{< var dfda_benefit_rd_only_annual >}}/year. That's **{{< var dfda_roi_rd_only >}}:1** on R&D savings alone, without counting a single human life. Include the lives (which you'd think someone would), and total societal benefit hits **{{< var treaty_roi_trial_capacity_plus_efficacy_lag >}}:1**.

Even the worst case (everything goes wrong, adoption is terrible, the servers catch fire) still returns an estimated 66:1. Your worst medical outcome is better than your best military one.
